sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Computer graphics is built on code. Large language model (LLM) agents can now generate graphics code and iteratively refine it through various feedback. This capability opens the door to a potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across a diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop a systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce a unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for human-agent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems.

This capability opens the door to potentially new paradigm of computer graphics, with graphics algorithms increasingly built around agentic systems to automate progressively complex tasks. Over the past years, research on agentic graphics has expanded rapidly across diverse range of tasks. This rapid growth makes it increasingly difficult for manual literature reviews to keep pace with new developments. At the same time, similar ideas are often described using different terminology across these tasks, further complicating efforts to develop systematic understanding of the field. In this report, we address these challenges through two contributions. First, we introduce unified taxonomy for characterizing agentic systems across diverse computer graphics tasks. Second, we develop an agentic literature system that can assist human researchers in analyzing existing and newly published papers at scale. Building on these contributions, we analyze emerging research trends and discuss open challenges in coordinating agents and tools across graphics tasks, designing interfaces and representations for humanagent collaboration, sustaining long-horizon planning and refinement, and reliably evaluating interactive graphics systems. 1. Introduction In computer graphics, code defines executable procedures for creating and manipulating visual content [Coo84; MWH*06]. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs), particularly their capabilities in code generation, reasoning, and tool use [CTJ*21; YZY*23], open up new opportunities for automating complex graphics workflows. By interacting with graphics environments, LLM agents can execute operations, inspect the results, and use feedback to guide subsequent actions [HYG24; HIJ*24; LCD*25]. We refer to systems that leverage these capabilities to perform computer graphics tasks as agentic graphics systems. Agentic graphics systems have demonstrated strong capabilities across diverse graphics tasks, including 3D asset creation and iterative 2 of 27 H. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics editing [LCD*25], articulated object animation [ZDH*26], and dynamic scene construction with rigid-body and fluid simulations [LWC*26]. For example, instead of manually specifying and adjusting shader programs [Coo84], users can guide an agents material edits with short language instruction and an optional reference image [HYG24]. The rapid growth of agentic graphics research (Fig. 2a), and the strong capabilities demonstrated by current agentic graphics systems motivate our survey. The demonstrated capabilities of these systems have attracted growing research interest across graphics applications. This expanding body of work poses challenges of both scale and terminology. First, the literature is large and growing at seemingly exponential rate: our collected corpus includes more than 300 papers published through September 2026 (Fig. 2a). This scale and pace of growth make it increasingly difficult to organize existing studies and synthesize the fields methods and findings. Second, studies across applications such as CAD, animation, and simulation describe functionally similar components using different terminology. Fig. 2b illustrates this variation in the names of feedback (top; Sec. 3.3.2) and planning (bottom; Sec. 3.3.1) modules. These differences can obscure shared design choices and complicate comparisons across works. These challenges make it difficult to assess the fields overall progress and identify broader research trends across graphics applications. To support coherent understanding of this rapidly growing field, we address these challenges through unified taxonomy and an agentic literature survey system built on it. First, we introduce taxonomy that characterizes agentic graphics systems along four dimensions: specification, base model, harness, and graphics interface and tooling  (Fig. 3)  . Within each dimension, we define the key design choices and provide common vocabulary for describing system components and their roles. This allows similarities and differences in system design to be examined across applications, even when individual works use different terminology. Second, we develop an agentic literature survey system that searches for relevant papers, reads their content, and annotates their designs using this taxonomy (Sec. 4). The system records taxonomy labels, design insights, and limitations alongside supporting source evidence, producing structured reports that support comparison across papers and analysis of broader research trends. By retaining these records across runs, it allows new papers to be incorporated and existing annotations to be revisited as further evidence becomes available. The taxonomy and the resulting literature analysis enable us to synthesize shared design patterns across applications (Secs. 6, 7, and 8), trace emerging research trends, and identify open challenges in agentic graphics (Sec. 9). We conclude by summarizing the surveys main findings (Sec. 10). 2. Background and Scope In this report, we study agentic systems that use large language models (LLMs) to perform computer graphics tasks. Here, we use the term LLM broadly, including models with visual capabilities or additional reasoning training. Such agentic graphics systems must satisfy three criteria: (1) an LLM makes at least some action decisions; (2) the system executes operations in graphics environment to create or modify graphics content; and (3) feedback on intermeFigure 2: Motivation for organizing the agentic graphics literature. (a) Rapid growth of our collected paper corpus. (b) Different names used across papers for feedback modules (top; Sec. 3.3.2) and planning modules (bottom; Sec. 3.3.1), motivating unified taxonomy for comparing system designs. diate graphics results or the execution of those operations is used to select or revise subsequent actions during the task. This definition is purposefully inclusive: we impose no restrictions on the graphics representation, software platform, training strategy, or level of automation. These actions can draw on broad range of tools, including image generators, renderers, simulators, and geometric solvers. We allow for diverse feedback sources, which may come from learned models, structured analysis, or human working with the system. We cover systems that generate, reconstruct, and edit graphics artifacts, across 2D media, as well as static and dynamic 3D content, including operations on materials, cameras, and lighting. At the same time, we use the above definition to set clear bounds on the scope of our report. The system must contain learned model capable of using tools and receiving feedback, which excludes many methods that train networks from scratch to directly solve graphics tasks. It also excludes single-pass LLM generation without subsequent feedback, and additionally methods that use feedback only for model training or final evaluation. Moreover, not all multi-step LLM pipelines are agentic, as the feedback stemming from the graphics environment must influence what actions the model takes. That said, an agentic workflow may still have predefined stages, provided the model is influenced by results of the previous stage. Comparison with Prior and Concurrent Surveys. Prior graphics surveys examine procedural modeling [STBB14], learned shape and scene structure [CRW*20], neural representations and rendering [XTS*22; TTM*22; KBM*20], and neurosymbolic modeling [RGJ*23]. These surveys establish the representations and construction methods that agentic graphics systems can use. Surveys of language model agents address general architectures [XCG*23; WMF*24], multimodal tool use [XCZ*24; YZH*25], software development and GUI interaction [LWC*24; DJQ*25; ZHQ*24; NCW*25], and runtime harnesses [MWC*26; LXZ*26a; TPC*26]. Recent surveys organize agentic visual creation by the scope of controller decisions [HTY*26], autonomy levels and functional components [XWX*26], or the agents role in generation, editing, composition, and programming [MHQ*26]. Across artifact doH. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics 3 of 27 mains, related work examines the interaction between representations, construction policies, and runtime verification [WHX*26]. Domain-specific surveys also review applications of language models to CAD [ZLA*26]. Our survey organizes agentic graphics systems through shared design space covering specification, base model, harness, graphics interface and tooling (Sec. 3). We examine how these choices interact across graphics tasks, with particular attention to how representations and available operations determine what agents can construct, inspect, and revise. The application sections (Sec. 6, 7, 8) use this design space to analyze how systems address the visual, geometric, and physical requirements of different graphics tasks. 2.1. Background Traditional Graphics Workflows. Graphics content is commonly authored through sequences of modeling, material, lighting, animation, and simulation operations, exposed through interactive interfaces or scripts. Procedural rules, shading programs, and numerical solvers automate geometry construction, appearance specification, and physical evolution [MWH*06; STBB14; Coo84; Sta99; ZPW*26].These workflows can also incorporate learned methods for shape and scene generation [CRW*20] and the inference of graphics programs from observations [RGJ*23]. Artists and engineers combine these capabilities, inspect rendered views or the underlying graphics state, and revise content, parameters, or programs to meet their goals. These workflows provide the representations, operations, and inspection mechanisms on which agentic graphics systems build. Learning to Generate Graphics Programs. Graphics programs can also be generated by specialized networks trained from scratch. Shape2Prog learns to infer programs from input shapes, using learned approximation of program execution to train the generator [TLS*19]. ShapeAssembly similarly learns hierarchical programs that construct shapes by connecting parts [JBX*20]. In both cases, the program describes how the shape is built, making its structure available for inspection and editing. These representations can support agentic workflows, but the generators themselves fall outside our scope because they do not use general-purpose LLM to decide which graphics operations to perform. Non-Agentic Uses of LLMs. LLMs can translate prompts and references into descriptions that specify graphics content. LayoutGPT [FZF*23] provides layouts for image and scene synthesis, while LLaMA-Mesh [WLW*24] generates mesh geometry as text. This approach also supports program generation: StarVector [RPA*25] produces SVG code, and UniCAD [CJS*26] generates executable CAD programs. In these settings, each candidate is generated in single pass, without iterative refinement based on execution feedback. Agentic systems use this feedback to guide subsequent construction or revision. Language Model Agents. Language model agents use an LLM to select actions based on task instructions and observations from an external environment [XCG*23]. surrounding software harness executes these actions through tools and returns their results to the model, connecting language-based decisions with external computation and interaction [SDD*23; YZY*23]. By retaining observations and feedback in context or memory, agents can revise plans, correct errors, and improve subsequent attempts without necessarily updating model weights [YZY*23; SCB*23]. These capabilities provide the basis for delegating parts of graphics authoring and revision to model while preserving access to existing graphics tools. 3. Design Space of Agentic Graphics Systems Building on the definition and scope established in Sec. 2, we introduce unified taxonomy that organizes the shared structure of agentic graphics systems  (Fig. 3)  . This taxonomy defines design space with four dimensions: specification, base model, harness, and graphics interface and tooling. The specification (Sec. 3.1) describes the task, available inputs, and expected outputs. Given these requirements, the base model(Sec. 3.2) makes decisions about how to proceed, while the harness(Sec. 3.3) coordinates planning, execution, feedback, and memory. The graphics interface and tooling(Sec. 3.4) provides the operations, resources, and representations needed to carry out the proposed actions. Within each dimension, we identify key design choices and denote each option with an icon. single system may combine several options for the same choice, such as using both rendered images and execution diagnostics as feedback. We reuse these icons in the application tables (Secs. 68), providing consistent notation for comparing methods across graphics tasks and connecting those comparisons to the definitions introduced here. 3.1. Specification Specification supplies the system with requirements and reference content that guide planning and generation. It is characterized by the target task, input form, and expected output. Task. Task specifies what activity the system should perform: . 2D Graphics creates or edits vector graphics, diagrams, data visualizations, posters, banners, presentations, and animations. (cid:229) Static 3D Graphics generates and manipulates 3D assets, such as parametric CAD constructs [LNC*26], Blender objects [LCD*25], material and texture modeling, and scene composition [PCZ*26]. Dynamic 3D Graphics specifies temporal changes in visual content, including object motion [ZWZT26; LWC*26], procedural particle effects [ZYW*26; ZWZT26], and camera motion [XWW*25]. It also involves constructing environments and behaviors governed by physical dynamics, including real-to-sim reconstruction [RWP*26; LXL*24], generation of simulation environments [XLL*26; PCZ*26], physical interactions [ZLL*26a; LWC*26], and articulated assets [ZLL*26b], Input Form. Input form describes the information and existing content supplied by the user: (cid:215) Language expresses intent and constraints [ZLL*26b]. º An image provides visual reference [YGW*26; KLC*26]. Video provides observations across views or time [RWP*26]. 4 of 27 H. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics Figure 3: Design Space of Agentic Graphics Systems. We taxonomize our design space into four dimensions: specification, base model, harness, graphics interface and tooling. We detail subclassification within each system following the taxonomy. (cid:243) An existing 3D representation supplies content for modification, such as Blender scenes with procedural geometry, material graphs, and lighting configurations [HYG24], or monolithic 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes that can be decomposed into individually editable objects [HGC*26]. document provides source content for graphics authoring, such as paper excerpts used to construct explanatory animations [JCS*26]. Output. Output specifies what content the system should return: program expresses construction operations as executable code, such as Python code for articulated part assembly [ZLL*26b], Blender scene-construction scripts [HIJ*24; LCD*25], or JavaScript game logic [JHX*26]. œ structured specification encodes components and relationships for graphics backend, such as JSON particle-system configurations [ZYW*26], CAD construction graphs with parameter dependencies [LNC*26], or URDF joints [ZLL*26b; LXL*24]. (cid:242) graphics artifact retains editable content, such as scenes with individually manipulable objects [HGC*26]. (cid:137) Rendered media encode the visual result as images or videos, such as explanatory animations [JCS*26] or rendered dynamic scenes [LWC*26]. 3.2. Base Model As the systems decision-making component, the base model reasons over user requirements and context supplied by the harness. It returns plans, code, or tool calls to the harness, which coordinates execution through graphics tools. Base models are characterized by model type and model training.

sections.content: Model Training. Model training describes how the base model is used or adapted: Off-the-shelf models are used without task-specific parameter updates [ZLL*26b; YGW*26]. (cid:135) Supervised fine-tuning adapts pretrained model using taskspecific inputoutput pairs, with training examples drawn from graphics programs [DCZ*24; GDN*26] or interaction trajectories [HAW*26]. (cid:140) Reinforcement-learning post-training optimizes the models policy to maximize task rewards. Rewards include geometric fidelity [HAW*26], sketch-token accuracy [YHHP26], and spatial validity [NYW*26]. 3.3. Harness The harness connects the base model to the graphics interface and tooling. It routes model decisions to graphics tools for execution and returns observations, assessments, and relevant memory to the model, allowing subsequent actions to respond to execution results. Here, we identify three sub-axes in the design space: planning and acting, feedback mechanisms, and memory. Model Type. Model type describes which models make decisions and what evidence they can interpret: 3.3.1. Plan & Act (cid:218) large language model (LLM) processes textual instructions, code, and tool reports, with implementations based on Qwen2.5-Coder [DCZ*24] or gpt-oss-120b [XLL*26]. Planning and acting organize the construction and revision of graphics artifacts. The base model uses task requirements and retained context to propose actions, which the harness schedules and H. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics 5 of 27 executes through the graphics interface. The harness returns execution feedback to the model for revision. This process is characterized by planning, workflow, and update strategy. Planning. Planning describes whether task plan is explicitly represented and how much of that plan is fixed in advance. We distinguish three levels, from more to less fixed: (cid:25) Hard-Coded prescribes the task steps and their order, leaving the model to carry out assigned steps [RWP*26; GHJ*25]. (cid:3) Hybrid combines predefined stages with model decisions about how to complete them, as in Articraft [ZLL*26b]. Non Hard-Coded lets the agent determine task steps and their order during execution, as in SAGE [XLL*26]. Workflow. Workflow describes how these steps are connected and scheduled, and specifies execution order and the flow of intermediate results: $ sequential workflow executes actions in order, passing each result to the next action [ZLL*26b; YGW*26]. (cid:214) parallel workflow executes independent subtasks concurrently, such as configuring separate particle emitters [ZYW*26] or furnishing different rooms [PCZ*26]. graph-structured workflow represents operations as nodes connected by dependencies or alternative branches. Structures include hierarchical task trees, such as roomfurnitureobject hierarchies that place supporting furniture before dependent objects [PCZ*26], and branching search trees, such as competing scene edits expanded and pruned over successive iterations [GHJ*25; HYG24]. Verifier. The verifier evaluates the graphics result using available evidence and returns an assessment to the harness: (cid:160) Self-verification has an agent assess its own output, for example by comparing rendered and target views [YGW*26] or tuninspecting simulated deformation during material ing [ZLL*26a]. critic employs separate agent, which may use the same underlying model as the acting agent, to assess outputs it did not create, such as indoor layouts [PCZ*26] or particle-effect appearance [ZYW*26]. Programmatic verification tests explicit constraints, such as geometric conditions or joint-extent checks [ZLL*26b]. (cid:211) Environment-based verification tests behavior through execution, such as object stability under gravity [XLL*26] or actor motion after simulation baking [LWC*26]. Human verification incorporates user judgments during refinement, such as critiques of generated assets [LCD*25] or feedback on intermediate game content [EPB24]. Feedback Signal. feedback signals are sourced either from assessment or environmental observation. Assessment expresses verifiers judgment of result: binary verdict indicates success or failure, for instance in geometric connectivity checks [ZLL*26b] TA score quantifies an artifacts quality, such as visual alignment [ZYW*26] or scene plausibility [PCZ*26] (cid:22)A ranking orders set of alternatives through pairwise comparisons [GHJ*25; HYG24] 3A diagnosis identifies defects, such as violated spatial constraints [XZY*26] or visual mismatches [YGW*26]. Update Strategy. Update strategy specifies how feedback changes the current plan or graphics artifact: Environmental observations report graphics state and execution behavior through tool outputs. These include: Regeneration replaces candidate in full, such as an animation script [JCS*26] or procedural modeling script [GSY*26]. local patch modifies selected components, such as particleemitter parameters [ZYW*26] or object placements [XZY*26]. (cid:153) Rollback restores an earlier state, such as reverting unsuccessful patch segments [ZYW*26] or restoring scene checkpoints after score decrease [PCZ*26]. Replanning revises intended steps, such as updating stages tactical plan [LWC*26] or changing refinement priorities and tool choices [YJZH25]. Candidate selection chooses among proposed updates, such as tournaments over edit scripts [GHJ*25] or pairwise tree search [HYG24]. 3.3.2. Feedback Mechanism º Visual observations, such as multi-view renders [YGW*26] or motion-frame sequences [LWC*26] (cid:243) Structural scene state, such as joint axes [ZLL*26b], or object poses and support relationships [PCZ*26] _ Runtime observations, such as compilation errors [ZYW*26] or physics-cache and bake states [LWC*26]. 3.3.3. Memory Memory stores information for reuse during task execution or across tasks. In an agentic graphics system, it connects the base model with task inputs, execution records from graphics tools, and assessments from the feedback mechanism. The harness stores selected information in memory and retrieves relevant records into the models context to inform subsequent decisions. Memory is characterized by retention time and access scope. The feedback mechanism links execution results to subsequent decisions. verifier assesses observations from the graphics environment against task requirements. The harness combines this assessment with the underlying observations into feedback signal, using it to control execution and guide the base models next action. The mechanism is characterized by the verifier and the feedback signal. Time. The temporal dimension describes how long information remains available for model decisions: Working memory is the context assembled for the current model call, such as task and tool instructions [ZLL*26b; XLL*26], or renders and plans [YGW*26; LWC*26]. 6 of 27 H. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics Short-term memory retains context across calls within run, such as revision histories [ZLL*26b; LCD*25] or render histories [YGW*26; PCZ*26]. ı Long-term memory stores knowledge for reuse across tasks without changing model weights, such as reusable skills [XZY*26; HIJ*24] or experience records [JCS*26; LNC*26]. Reach. Reach specifies the scope within which stored information can be retrieved for model decisions: Local memory is accessible only within an individual execution context, such as separate designer and critic histories [PCZ*26], or stage-specific sessions [LWC*26; PCZ*26]. Global memory makes common store of information accessible across execution contexts, such as shared conversation histories [LCD*25], requirement-status records [XZY*26], or scene representations reused across stages [XZY*26; YLG*26]. Combining both scopes preserves specialized context while supporting coordination. 3.4. Graphics Interface & Tooling An agent interacts with graphics software through instructions that create, inspect, or modify graphics content. The available operations depend on the software environment, the content representation, and the tools and resources provided to the agent. We examine these choices along five dimensions: action type, graphics environment, representation, tools, and resources. 3.4.1. Action Type Action type describes the form in which an agent specifies an operation for execution. We distinguish four types: code/script, structured specification, tool/function call, and GUI action. These types differ in how much of an operation the agent must specify and how much is handled by the execution environment. Code/Scripts. The agent generates or modifies executable programs that construct or edit graphics content. Programs combine graphics API calls with variables, loops, and functions, giving the agent control over operation order, repetition, and parameter dependencies. Applications include procedural modeling and scene layout [SHD*25; HIJ*24], material and lighting editing [HYG24], parametric CAD modeling [BLF26], and articulated object construction [ZLL*26b; LXL*24]. Generated code may contain syntax or API errors, and successful execution does not guarantee that the resulting content satisfies the task requirements. œ Structured Specification. The agent describes graphics content or edits using predefined schema, which an interpreter, solver, or converter translates into graphics operations. Examples include particle-system specifications [ZYW*26], indoor scene layout [BRYC25; ÇHS*24; WCR*26], and template-defined slide components [FWZ26]. The execution layer handles construction, while the agent controls the entities, relationships, and parameters exposed by the schema. Edits through this interface are therefore limited to those the schema can express. (cid:229) Tool/Function Call. The agent selects predefined operation and supplies its arguments. Calls support scene construction and editing [XLL*26; YJZH25; PCZ*26], geometry inspection and rendering [SGK*26], and spatial evaluation, including circulation and clearance checks [WCR*26]. The agent determines which operations to invoke and in what order, while each tool implements the requested operation. This reduces the implementation detail the agent must generate, but limits direct control to the operations and parameters exposed by the interface. GUI Action. The agent operates graphics software through mouse and keyboard input, including clicks, drags, shortcuts, and text entry. Applications include building and mechanical modeling [DDNB25; DLM*26], and image and video editing [TZX*24; WXN*26]. GUI actions provide access to existing interactive workflows, but require the agent to locate interface elements and track application state. The effect of an action can depend on the current selection, active editing mode, or open dialog. system may combine several action types. We classify actions by the graphics instruction rather than the mechanism used to submit it: script passed to an execution tool remains code action, and mouse or keyboard commands remain GUI actions when encoded as function calls. 3.4.2. Graphics Software The graphics environment provides the runtime and interfaces through which an agent constructs, edits, and inspects graphics content. We distinguish agent-native environments, agent-adapted environments, and direct use of general-purpose software according to how support for agent interaction is provided. This distinction concerns the environment configuration used by each system. Source availability, API coverage, and documentation access are considered separately, since they can vary within each category. Agent-native. The authoring interface, state representation, and execution feedback are designed together for agent use. Examples include dedicated SDKs for defining geometry, parts, and joints [ZLL*26b], domain-specific languages with relational operators for composing geometry [WWH*26], and scene-authoring runtimes that combine local operations with explicit state and constraint verification [XZY*26]. Construction and validation operate on shared task entities, such as named parts or scene objects, allowing the agent to relate execution feedback to the target content. (cid:148) Agent-adapted. An existing graphics environment is extended with dedicated interface for agent operations and state inspection. The added layer translates requests into application-specific operations and returns structured state or diagnostic feedback. Examples include scene and simulation inspection in Blender [YGW*26; LWC*26], and geometry queries and edit-history management in CAD environments [SGK*26]. The underlying software supplies the graphics capabilities, while the adapter determines how those capabilities and their results are exposed to the agent. ł General-purpose. The agent uses existing scripting APIs, procedural libraries, file formats, or GUI workflows without dedicated authoring abstraction for agents. Examples include graphH. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics 7 of ics editing through Blenders Python interface [GHJ*25], mathematical animation through Manim [JCS*26], and CAD or building modeling through application GUIs [DLM*26; DDNB25]. The agent must follow the softwares conventions for addressing content, specifying operations, and interpreting state. generic script executor or GUI-control wrapper does not by itself make the environment agent-adapted. Source availability, API coverage, and documentation access are separate properties across all three categories. Access to source code supports inspection and modification of the implementation, while documented APIs may also be available in closed-source software. Human editing and agent control may coexist within the same environment. 3.4.3. Tools Tools provide callable capabilities for acting on or inspecting graphics content. We distinguish graphics operations, perception models, and validators according to the functions they provide within graphics workflow. This dimension describes the capabilities available to the agent, while action type describes how operations are expressed and graphics software specifies the environment in which they execute. (cid:20) Graphics Operations. Graphics operations create or modify 3D graphics state through authoring functions. These include constructing geometry, changing object transforms and materials, and defining part relationships or motion controls. VIGA [YGW*26] uses Blender operations to construct geometry and revise scene layout, while Articraft [ZLL*26b] provides dedicated operations for composing part geometry and specifying joints. The available operations determine the granularity of editing: an agent may adjust individual parameters, modify an existing object, or construct an assembly through sequence of calls. Their execution updates the graphics state that subsequent observations and checks inspect.

sections.content: (cid:192) Validators. Validators assess graphics content against specified requirements and may compute states satisfying geometric or physical constraints. Solver validators explore alternative states through optimization or simulation, potentially returning revised configuration. SceneThesis [LLL*26], for example, adjusts object poses under collision and support constraints, while physics simulators can test stability by evolving scene under gravity. Static validators inspect the supplied state directly, checking properties such as intersections, unsupported objects, or mesh watertightness. For presentation graphics, PosterMELD [HDL*26] applies checks to layout bounds, overlap, and text size. These checks identify violations that subsequent edits can address without prescribing how the content should be revised. These categories can overlap within single tool. In this way, VLM may extract information from rendered views or assess whether visual requirement is satisfied, while constraint solver may both diagnose violations and modify scene state. 3.4.4. Resources Resources comprise reusable graphics content and reference knowledge available during authoring. They may be incorporated into the output or consulted to guide construction and repair. We distinguish three categories: assets, examples and experience, and documentation and rules. (cid:226) Assets. Assets provide reusable geometry, materials, and other graphics components. Examples include object meshes from BlenderKit and Poly Haven [ZLL*26a], scene objects from Objaverse and 3D-FUTURE [YJZH25], and articulated models from ArtVIP and surface materials from ambientCG [PCZ*26]. Asset reuse reduces construction effort, while the available part structure, joint definitions, and physical properties affect subsequent editing and simulation. _ Examples & Trajectories. Examples and trajectories provide construction patterns and diagnostic knowledge that can guide new tasks. These include articulated-modeling code examples [ZLL*26b], CAD construction graphs and reusable subgraphs [LNC*26], diagnostic cases linking visual symptoms to particle-system errors [ZYW*26], and success rationales and failure lessons from animation generation [JCS*26]. Such resources may be curated in advance or accumulated from completed tasks, then supplied as context or retrieved during construction and repair. [ Documentation & Rules. Documentation and rules describe supported operations, parameter meanings, and requirements for valid use. Examples include Blender API references [LCD*25], CadQuery documentation and modeling guidelines [AAMJ26], and version-specific Blender schemas and manuals [LWC*26]. These references guide operation selection and argument specification. Their usefulness depends on coverage of the required operations and consistency with the target software version. These categories describe resource content, while access and maintenance are separate design choices. Resources may be supplied in advance or retrieved on demand, and may remain fixed or be updated as the system accumulates experience. 3.4.5. Representation Representation describes how graphics content is encoded for editing, simulation, and observation. It determines which entities and properties can be addressed by operations or exposed through feedback. We distinguish six overlapping forms according to the information they retain. Code. To automatically identify new and relevant papers, our agent first scans publication listings and searches the web using customized queries [NHB*21]. The query can be iteratively refined based on retrieval results, following the framework in ReAct [YZY*23]. Throughout this process, the system maintains list of candidate papers by identifying and merging related works, removing duplicates, and verifying publication versions against official sources. The agent then reviews the abstracts of selected candidate papers, prioritizing full-text reading based on the date cutoff and available budget, while deferring uncertain or unread candidates to subsequent runs. Evidence-based annotation. Once paper is selected, the agent reads its text and inspects relevant figures and tables using dedicated tools [YJW*24]. Following PaperQA2 [SCL*24], the agent gathers supporting evidence before classifying the work. Based on this evidence, it identifies how the main agent interacts with graphics content, determines whether the paper falls within the scope of the survey, and assigns taxonomy labels. The agent classifies each paper according to our unified taxonomy, ensuring consistent categorization across works despite minor differences in terminology. The generated annotation retains source references, distinguishes reported facts from the agents interpretations, and separates training, inference, and evaluation procedures. The agent also flags cases with insufficient supporting evidence. Knowledge curation. To enable reuse and refinement in subsequent runs, the system maintains curated record of paper versions, annotations, and supporting evidence, independent of the agents temporary working context [SYNG24]. Before saving each annotation, the system verifies that all required fields are present and that the assigned labels adhere to the taxonomy. We note that while these checks identify missing or inconsistent entries, they do not verify the correctness of the classifications. When work is flagged for insufficient supporting evidence, the agent can revisit the paper within the allocated budget. Each paper is saved independently to preserve progress in case of interruptions, allowing subsequent runs to resume from unresolved candidates and revisit existing annotations when new versions or evidence become available. 4.2. Search Analysis Our agentic literature survey system enables us to systematically analyze large body of existing works using our proposed taxonomy, providing new insights into common patterns and emerging trends across the literature  (Fig. 5)  . Our analysis reveals several notable patterns, four of which we discuss below. (1) Feedback observations: Visual feedback is the most widely used observation type, appearing in 77.0% of the 304 works that use observation as feedback (Fig. 5a). This is expected given the rapid development of VLMs, which enable agents to interpret outputs and provide feedback without task-specific visual evaluators. 58.2% combine multiple observation categories, suggesting that single observation type may be often insufficient. For instance, geometric measurements and simulations provide additional information about structural and physical validity that may not be apparent from visual feedback alone [BLF26; CZS*26]. The choice of feedback also varies across tasks: scene generation accounts for the largest share of assignments involving visual and structural observations (Fig. 5a.1, a.3), whereas CAD generation accounts for the largest share involving runtime observations(Fig. 5a.2). This difference may reflect the greater emphasis on geometric precision and executable correctness in CAD workflows. (2) Update strategies: Different tasks utilize different approaches to revising generated outputs. CAD generation more frequently relies on full regeneration, whereas scene generation more frequently uses local patch updates (Fig. 5b.2). One possible explanation is that scene representations often allow individual objects and their properties to be modified independently, while CAD operations can involve dependencies between modeling steps, making local modifications more challenging. Beyond choosing how to update an artifact, some systems also evaluates whether revision should be retained. For example, SceneSmith [PCZ*26], restores previous checkpoints when critic scores decline, allowing unsuccessful updates to be reversed. (3) Supporting resources: The type of assets systems utilize also differ across tasks (Fig. 5c.2). Open Problems In this report, we review the emerging landscape of agentic graphics workflows, formally defining their scope and examining the capabilities that enable agents to create and edit visual content. We develop taxonomy of existing systems and organize recent advances across range of domains, including computer graphics, computer vision, CAD, 2D graphics, and human-computer interaction. This taxonomy reveals common patterns and shared capabilities across different approaches, while also shedding light on gaps and underexplored areas that warrant further investigation. Building on this analysis, we discuss key open problems and opportunities for advancing the field of agentic graphics. Multi-agent collaboration and cross-task generalization Graphics agents are evolving from task-specific systems with predefined workflows toward more general frameworks capable of handling complex tasks across modalities and applications. As we move to more complex tasks that require effective collaboration, this will require agents to dynamically decompose objectives, coordinate specialized expertise, and integrate intermediate results into coherent artifact. Beyond coordinating agents within single workflow, an important challenge is enabling collaboration across various tools and domains, where representations and assumptions may not be directly compatible. Future work should investigate how agents can share knowledge, transfer skills across tasks, and adapt their collaboration strategies to unfamiliar requirements, rather than relying on manually designed pipelines for each application. Action spaces and tool orchestration. Visual generation agents increasingly operate through heterogeneous interfaces, including code generation, GUI interactions, API calls, and domain-specific programs. These action spaces offer complementary capabilities: code enables precise, reproducible modifications, while GUI interactions provide access to functionality that may not be exposed programmatically. As agentic systems expand to more diverse applications, key challenge is determining which actions and tools are appropriate for given task, when to switch between them, and how to combine them within single workflow. Although recent works 20 of H. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics have begun to move beyond fixed tool-use strategies toward adaptive orchestration, selecting and coordinating actions across heterogeneous interfaces while balancing execution reliability, editability, and cost remains an open challenge. An interesting research directions could be to study what is the optimal kind of action and tools for an given application and agentic graphic system. Agent-oriented interfaces and representations. Many existing graphics tools and domain-specific languages (DSLs) were designed primarily for human use, and may not provide the most effective abstractions for agents to reason about and manipulate visual content. promising direction is to develop agent-oriented languages and interfaces that facilitate more effective agent execution and inter-agent communication. For instance, an effective abstractions could enable agents to express, exchange, and compose actions and intermediate representations with minimal ambiguity. For example, AIDL [JZH*25] introduces hierarchical, solver-aided language for CAD that aligns with the strengths of language models by representing high-level structure explicitly and offloading geometric constraints to solver. Beyond manually designing such languages, future agents could learn to identify, compose, or even develop task-specific languages and neural primitives that serve as reusable building blocks for visual actions and interactions. However, representations optimized for agent reasoning and execution may not align with what is intuitive or interpretable to human designers. Bridging this gap will require interfaces that translate between machine-oriented representations and human-understandable concepts, preserving the efficiency and flexibility of agent-native operations while enabling users to inspect, understand, and edit the resulting artifacts. Long-horizon planning, memory, and efficiency. Visual design is inherently iterative. Human designers typically develop an initial concept and progressively refine it by evaluating intermediate results and revisiting earlier decisions. Such iterative workflows rely on retaining and reusing intermediate results, design decisions, tools, and assets across multiple iterations. Enabling agents to follow similar process becomes increasingly important as generation tasks grow more complex and involve interdependent decisions, multiple rounds of generations, and accumulated design constraints. Agents must maintain project state across iterations, track design decisions and dependencies, and preserve intermediate outputs for subsequent refinement. Beyond retaining context, they should learn from failed attempts, reuse successful strategies, and develop new procedures as requirements change. Without such capabilities, early mistakes can propagate through later stages, making corrections increasingly costly. Moving forward, the community should explore how to build agentic systems that continuously learn from their own outputs and performance, enabling them to adapt, refine their strategies while balancing design quality with computational costs. Transparency and Interpretability. Agentic workflows can be difficult to understand when intermediate decisions and operations remain hidden behind final output. Exposing plans, assumptions, intermediate artifacts, and edit histories would allow users to inspect how result was produced and identify the source of errors. Making these processes understandable without overwhelming users with low-level execution details is an important yet unsolved problem. Effective transparency should support both retrospective inspection and intervention during generation, enabling users to understand not only what changed but also why. Human interaction and intent alignment. User requests are often incomplete, ambiguous, or expressed in subjective terms such as make it cleaner" or move the stars lower". Without shared conceptual grounding between users and agents, such instructions are difficult to interpret, evaluate, and follow precisely, as users and agents may have different understandings of the intended outcome. Following user instructions requires agents to determine when to infer reasonable defaults, when to expose their assumptions, and when to ask for necessary clarification questions. This is particularly important in graphics, where instructions are often underspecified and multiple visually or structurally distinct outputs may satisfy the same request, making it difficult to distinguish intended design choices from incorrect assumptions. An important direction is to develop interaction strategies that combine proactive clarification, explicit assumption management, and fine-grained human feedback, allowing users to steer the generation process without specifying every implementation detail. An emerging direction in this space studies systems where people and LLMs first work together to build user-centric common vocabulary of reusable operations that improve alignment on future tasks [JGMR26; JWA26] Reliable evaluation and validation Assessing generated visual artifacts remains challenging because visual quality involves multiple dimensions, including semantic correctness, spatial relationships, aesthetic quality, and domain-specific validity. While VLMs are often used as critics, these models are known to overlook subtle errors, not align well with human perception, or be insensitive to violations of physical and geometric constraints [KHC23; CXK*24]. Beyond assessing individual artifacts, evaluating agentic graphics systems introduces additional challenges. First, the stochastic nature of agentic workflows can lead to substantial variation across runs, making it difficult to draw reliable conclusions from limited number of evaluations. Second, many systems rely on proprietary foundation models, making it challenging to disentangle improvements arising from agentic system design from those attributable to the underlying models. Additionally, evaluation at scale remains difficult, as assessing the quality of graphics artifacts often requires specialized expertise and time-consuming human inspection. These challenges call for not only stronger benchmarks but also evaluation protocols that enable reliable and scalable assessment of both artifact and agentic behavior. Creativity and attribution As visual agents take on increasingly substantial roles in ideation, composition, and refinement, their place within creative workflows becomes less clear. Rather than treating generation as binary distinction between humanand machine-produced work, future research should examine how creative decisions are distributed between users and agents, how human direction shapes the resulting artifact, and how generated contributions should be attributed. This raises broader questions about authorship, provenance, and accountability, particularly when outputs incorporate user-provided materials, retrieved references, or assets generated across multiple tools. Supporting transH. Liu et al. / Advances in Agentic Computer Graphics 21 of 27 parent provenance and meaningful human control will be important for integrating agentic systems into professional and academic design practice. 10. Conclusion In this survey, we treat agentic graphics as class of systems in which base model performs graphics operations through agentic harness in graphics interface (Sec. 2). The literature that meets this definition is growing quickly and across communities that do not share vocabulary  (Fig. 2)  . Our survey addresses such challenges by constructing unified taxonomy that categorizes various works according to four dimensions: user input, base model, harness, and graphics interface and tooling (Sec. 3). To automate this process, we also provide an agentic system that can conduct literature search to discover candidate works, annotate it with the taxonomy, and retain records adaptively (Sec. 4). We also evaluate benchmarks (Sec. 5) and agentic graphics systems spanning various dimensions and tasks: 2D graphics, static 3D assets, and dynamic 3D assets (Secs. 6, 7, and 8). Finally, we discuss potential directions for the field and open problems (Sec. 9). Our survey reveals several key insights into the current landscape of agentic graphics systems. Across different tasks, we observe recurring design patterns, particularly in how systems approach planning, verification, and iterative refinement. Most existing systems rely on off-the-shelf base models, with relatively limited exploration of supervised or reinforcement post-training tailored to graphics tasks. In contrast, harness designs exhibit considerably greater diversity, reflecting different strategies for orchestrating agentic workflows and incorporating feedback. We also find that code and structured specifications remain the dominant forms of interaction with graphics environments, while tool calls and GUI actions are adopted depending on the available interfaces. Finally, evaluation practices are gradually expanding beyond final artifact quality to consider multi-step editing, interaction trajectories, and the effectiveness of agentic workflows. Given the rapid growth of agentic graphics research, establishing unified taxonomy is increasingly important for organizing and comparing systems developed across different communities, particularly as new tools, interfaces, and agentic mechanisms continue to emerge. We envision our taxonomy as an adaptive framework whose high-level structure can accommodate future developments, while individual design dimensions and categories can be expanded and refined as new approaches emerge. We hope this survey provides common vocabulary and foundation for understanding existing approaches, identifying emerging trends, and guiding the development of more capable, reliable, and generalizable agentic graphics systems.
